overview: This breakout pairs an MCP2515 CAN controller (which handles the CAN protocol — framing, arbitration, error detection — but has no bus-electrical drive capability of its own) with a CAN transceiver chip (typically TJA1050-class) that actually drives the CANH/CANL differential pair. The host microcontroller talks to the MCP2515 over SPI and never sees the raw bus electrical signaling directly. CAN's defining feature versus a simple point-to-point serial link is multi-drop bus arbitration: multiple nodes can attempt to transmit at the same time, and the bus's dominant/recessive bit scheme lets the highest-priority message win without corrupting anyone's data, no collision retry needed like on a shared Ethernet segment. This is why CAN is the backbone of automotive networks and increasingly of multi-node robot subsystems (per-joint motor controllers, distributed sensor nodes) where dozens of devices need to share one twisted pair reliably.
simpleSummary: A breakout board that lets a microcontroller talk on a CAN bus, the same multi-device wiring standard cars use to link their onboard computers.

specifications.transceiverChip: TJA1050-class CAN transceiver (some boards use MCP2551)
specifications.onboardOscillator: 8 MHz or 16 MHz crystal (board-dependent — must match library configuration)
specifications.operatingVoltage: 5V logic on most boards (some 3.3V transceiver variants exist)
specifications.busTopology: multi-drop linear bus, 120 ohm termination required at both physical ends only
specifications.practicalNodeLimit: up to ~112 nodes per segment (standard transceiver electrical load limit)

pinMap.name: VCC
pinMap.function: Power input for both the MCP2515 controller and the onboard CAN transceiver.
pinMap.gotcha: Even when the MCP2515's own SPI logic tolerates 3.3V, many boards' transceiver is 5V-only — check the specific board's transceiver datasheet before assuming 3.3V compatibility, rather than just checking the controller chip.

pinMap.name: GND
pinMap.function: Ground reference, shared with the host microcontroller.

pinMap.name: CS
pinMap.function: SPI chip-select input, active LOW, selects this device for each SPI transaction.
pinMap.gotcha: Must be driven by a GPIO the SPI library explicitly controls per transaction — leaving it permanently grounded to 'simplify wiring' breaks any attempt to share the SPI bus with another device later.

pinMap.name: SO
pinMap.function: SPI data output (MISO), module to host.

pinMap.name: SI
pinMap.function: SPI data input (MOSI), host to module.

pinMap.name: INT
pinMap.function: Interrupt output, active LOW, asserted when a CAN message has been received or another controller event is pending.
pinMap.gotcha: Polling status registers over SPI instead of wiring this pin works but wastes SPI bandwidth continuously checking for new frames — on a busy bus this can start missing messages that a hardware interrupt would have caught immediately.

pinMap.name: CANH
pinMap.function: CAN bus differential line, high side, driven by the onboard transceiver.
pinMap.gotcha: Unlike a UART TX/RX pair, two nodes driving this simultaneously don't corrupt each other's data — CAN's bitwise arbitration lets the higher-priority (lower ID) message win cleanly. The far more common real-world failure is simply missing 120 ohm termination at the two physical bus ends, which causes reflections and corrupted frames that get worse at higher bitrates and longer cable runs.

pinMap.name: CANL
pinMap.function: CAN bus differential line, low side, paired with CANH.
pinMap.gotcha: Swapping CANH/CANL doesn't usually damage anything but inverts the dominant/recessive sense, generally resulting in zero valid frames rather than garbled ones — a clean, total silence is a good clue to check this pair.

useCases.title: Automotive OBD-II data logging
useCases.scenario: Read live engine/vehicle data broadcast on the car's CAN bus for a datalogger or dashboard project.

useCases.title: Multi-node robot subsystem network
useCases.scenario: Give each joint or subsystem board its own CAN node so a single twisted pair carries commands and telemetry for the whole robot instead of dozens of point-to-point wires, similar to how many modern smart motor controllers communicate.

useCases.title: Industrial sensor bus retrofit
useCases.scenario: Replace dozens of individual analog sensor wire runs on a machine with a single CAN bus carrying all sensor readings as periodic broadcast messages.

useCases.title: Two-board CAN link prototype
useCases.scenario: Wire two Arduinos with CAN modules directly to each other on a short bus to learn frame IDs, filters, and arbitration before deploying a full multi-node network.

useCases.title: BMS cell-monitoring board integration
useCases.scenario: Have a battery management system board report pack voltage, current, and cell balancing status over CAN to a central vehicle or robot controller.

oftenConfusedWith: RS-485/Modbus module — also a differential multi-drop bus, but Modbus RTU is strictly master-polled request/response with no arbitration, whereas CAN allows any node to transmit and resolves collisions itself via built-in bitwise arbitration, CRC error checking, and automatic retransmission

Plain UART/serial link — point-to-point only, no multi-master capability; a single stuck-dominant node can jam an entire CAN bus in a way that has no equivalent failure mode on a simple two-wire UART link
oftenUpgradedTo: CAN FD controllers for higher throughput (up to 8 Mbps in the data phase)
SocketCAN-based Linux CAN interfaces for higher-level networking stacks and tooling

beginnerMistakes: Forgetting termination resistors at both physical bus ends (not at every node) — an unterminated or over-terminated bus both cause reflection problems.

Mismatching the library's assumed crystal frequency (commonly 8 MHz) against the board's actual onboard crystal (often 16 MHz), causing bit-timing errors that show up as sporadic frame corruption instead of total failure.
Wiring CANH/CANL directly into a hobbyist 5V logic pin thinking it's just another serial line — it's a transceiver-driven differential bus, not a TTL signal.
Running nodes at different bitrates on the same bus — every node must agree on an identical bitrate or none of them see valid frames.
Ignoring SPI chip-select conflicts when stacking multiple SPI devices (this module plus an SD card, display, etc.) on one host.
